title: Conflict Resolution

jokes.text: No. 'Cause I'm in a band. We really rock.
jokes.setup: Someone asks Pam if she's found a band for her wedding yet.
jokes.punchline: Pam casually reveals she's in a band and says 'We really rock' with total sincerity, which plays as absurd given the mundane office setting.
jokes.explanation: A mild character comedy beat. The joke is Pam's flat sincerity about being in a band — it's a small character detail delivered with deadpan confidence. Functional but not especially inventive.

jokes.text: We both have to hear Dwight order deer urine over the Internet.
jokes.setup: Jim is doing a talking head about how he and Pam overhear each other's conversations — she hears his social life, he hears her wedding planning.
jokes.punchline: He introduces the third element: both of them have to hear Dwight ordering deer urine online, which levels the complaint field with an absurd escalation.
jokes.explanation: This works beautifully because it uses Dwight's well-established hunting obsession and weaponizes it as comic relief in what would otherwise be a mundane complaint. The specificity of 'deer urine' and 'over the Internet' — two layers of specificity — elevates it. Strong character integration: only Dwight would do this, and only Jim would observe it this drily.

jokes.text: I don't want anyone there who has called me a hussy.
jokes.setup: Pam explains she didn't invite a few people to her wedding, which might make things awkward.
jokes.punchline: The reason is absurdly specific and archaic — someone called her a 'hussy' — implying this is a known fact about a specific person (Angela) without naming them.
jokes.explanation: The word 'hussy' is doing enormous work here — it's an antiquated, prissy insult that instantly points to Angela without naming her, and Pam delivers it with complete seriousness. The rewatch bonus comes from knowing the Angela/Pam dynamic. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Yes, thanks. Fantastic Sams, Adult Cut Plus. Comes with a shampoo and blow-dry.
jokes.setup: Michael is getting his photo ID taken and is clearly treating it as a glamour event.
jokes.punchline: He brags about getting a haircut at Fantastic Sams — a budget chain — and the 'Adult Cut Plus' upgrade, delivered with the pride of someone who went to a high-end salon.
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael Scott self-aggrandizement about something utterly mundane. The specificity of 'Fantastic Sams' (a discount chain) vs. his pride sells the joke. Solid character comedy but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Dwight wearing clown paint for his ID photo — 'What is on your face? Is that a disguise?' 'Clown paint.'
jokes.setup: The office is getting ID badge photos taken. Michael asks about something clearly visible on Dwight's face.
jokes.punchline: Dwight has painted his face in clown makeup, presumably as a 'disguise,' and calls it 'clown paint' with complete seriousness.
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Dwight in clown paint for a security badge is deeply on-brand — his paranoia about security leads him to a disguise that is maximally conspicuous. The deadpan delivery of 'Clown paint' as a self-evident answer is very funny. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Last year I came to work with my spud gun in a duffel bag. I sat at my desk all day with a rifle that shoots potatoes at 60 pounds per square inch. Can you imagine if I was deranged?
jokes.setup: Dwight is making a talking-head about office security being inadequate.
jokes.punchline: He describes having essentially smuggled a potato-shooting weapon into the office and sat with it all day, then asks 'Can you imagine if I was deranged?' — the joke being that this IS deranged behavior.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent. The joke operates on multiple levels: Dwight genuinely believes he proved a security point, while simultaneously proving he is the security threat. The self-awareness gap — 'Can you imagine if I was deranged?' said by someone who just described sitting at a desk all day with a weapon — is perfectly constructed. Only Dwight can deliver this with complete sincerity. The dark subversion is earned, not gratuitous.

jokes.text: Michael asking to borrow the photographer's tie for his ID photo.
jokes.setup: Michael compliments the photographer's tie and asks who makes it.
jokes.punchline: He then asks if he can wear it for his ID photo — a completely inappropriate and socially bizarre request from a stranger.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy. Michael's social obliviousness is on display but it's a minor beat — the photographer's flat refusal ('Let's keep our clothes') is the best part.

jokes.text: Oscar's meltdown: 'It's like child abuse! I say, if Jesus saw that, he'd freak out! He'd freak out, Toby! I mean, on so many levels!'
jokes.setup: Oscar is venting to Toby about a poster in his workspace featuring babies posed as adults.
jokes.punchline: His reaction escalates to invoking Jesus having a freakout, delivered with genuine outrage about what is ultimately a kitschy baby poster.
jokes.explanation: The disproportionate outrage is funny, and 'He'd freak out, Toby' has a nice specificity of address. The escalation is the engine here. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I forget, are you guys dating?' after learning Oscar and Angela are in a dispute.
jokes.setup: Toby explains that Angela and Oscar are having a dispute over a poster.
jokes.punchline: Michael's bizarre response is to ask if they're dating — completely tone-deaf and irrelevant.
jokes.explanation: A mild Michael obliviousness beat. Functional but thin.

jokes.text: Michael: 'What do you know about conflict resolution? Your answer to everything is to get divorced.'
jokes.setup: Toby explains his passive, listen-and-forget approach to HR conflict resolution.
jokes.punchline: Michael dismisses Toby's expertise by bringing up his divorce as a blanket disqualification.
jokes.explanation: This is a strong Michael/Toby exchange. Michael's contempt for Toby is one of the show's great recurring dynamics, and weaponizing Toby's divorce as a disqualifier for conflict expertise is both cruel and perfectly Michael. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Michael: 'In this office it is till death do us part. Assuming that we don't get downsized.'
jokes.setup: Michael is telling Toby that divorce-style solutions won't work in the office.
jokes.punchline: He makes a grandiose loyalty statement and immediately qualifies it with the mundane corporate threat of downsizing.
jokes.explanation: A nice self-undermining beat. Michael's grandiose speech deflates itself mid-sentence. Solid structure.

jokes.text: Michael holds up a book titled 'A Mediators Toolchest' — a visual gag of him having a novelty conflict resolution manual.
jokes.setup: Michael is about to lead a conflict resolution session with Angela and Oscar.
jokes.punchline: He has come prepared with an actual mediator's handbook, implying he found this and thinks he's now an expert — typical Michael.
jokes.explanation: A minor visual character beat. It sets up the mediation sequence but isn't especially funny on its own.

jokes.text: Michael doing a mock Asian accent: 'My Shaolin temple style defeats your monkey style.'
jokes.setup: Michael is introducing the 'five styles of conflict' from his handbook.
jokes.punchline: He responds to the martial-arts-coded language of conflict 'styles' with a racist kung fu movie impression.
jokes.explanation: This is classic Michael Scott cringe — the joke is his casual racism and inappropriate behavior, which is on-brand. However, the bit itself is fairly cheap; the mock accent is a shortcut. Character integration saves it from being actively bad, but it's a weak joke.

jokes.text: Michael explaining lose-lose by saying 'You would both lose' — drawing out the explanation with comic earnestness.
jokes.setup: Michael is explaining the first conflict style (lose-lose) in painstaking detail.
jokes.punchline: He repeats 'you would both lose' and then solemnly asks if they want to pursue a lose-lose negotiation — treating an obvious tautology as a serious mediation technique.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Michael's procedural earnestness about something self-evident. The sustained awkward pause where no one answers is the real joke. Functional cringe.

jokes.text: Win-win is number four. And number five is win-win-win. The important difference here is with win-win-win, we all win. Me, too. I win for having successfully mediated a conflict at work.
jokes.setup: Angela cuts to the chase and asks about win-win. Michael corrects her that win-win is only number four.
jokes.punchline: Win-win-WIN is number five, and Michael explains that HE also wins — specifically for having mediated — making the entire framework about his own ego.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The win-win-win concept is a perfect encapsulation of Michael's narcissism dressed up as management philosophy. He has genuinely reframed conflict resolution as a framework for his own glory. The escalation from win-win (a real concept) to win-win-win (his invention) is well-structured, and the reveal that the third 'win' is just him feeling good about himself is both absurd and completely character-specific. Highly quotable, became a recurring joke in the show's lexicon.

jokes.text: Angela's defense of the baby poster: 'It makes me feel like the babies are the true artists, and God has a really cute sense of humor.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks Angela to use 'I' language to express her feelings about the baby poster.
jokes.punchline: Angela's sincere defense is that the babies are the 'true artists' and that God has a cute sense of humor — a deeply earnest and slightly unhinged spiritual reading of kitsch.
jokes.explanation: Angela's prim religious sincerity applied to a cheesy baby poster is perfect character comedy. The idea that God's 'cute sense of humor' is evidenced by babies in business suits is a funny theological leap. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Oscar's counter-attack: 'It's kitsch. It's the opposite of art. It destroys art, it destroys souls.' Then: 'This is so much more offensive to me than hard-core porn.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is asked to respond to Angela's defense of the baby poster.
jokes.punchline: His escalating critique reaches its apex with the comparison to hardcore pornography — the baby poster is MORE offensive to him than porn, delivered with total conviction.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is excellent — 'destroys art, destroys souls' sets up a pompous register that then gets subverted by the porn comparison. It's funny because Oscar is clearly an aesthete with real opinions, but the comparison is so extreme it becomes absurd. Strong character integration for Oscar as the cultured, passionate one. The line 'so much more offensive to me than hard-core porn' is close to quotable.

jokes.text: Michael's win-win solution: Angela makes the poster into a t-shirt, which Oscar wears — so he can never see it, and whenever she looks at him she can see it.
jokes.setup: Michael asks everyone to brainstorm 'creative alternatives' to resolve the poster dispute.
jokes.punchline: His solution is so convoluted it circles back to being worse for everyone — Oscar has to wear a shirt with the image he hates, which Michael calls 'win-win-win.'
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke. Michael's 'solution' is so profoundly stupid that it takes a moment to fully parse — Oscar would be WEARING the image he finds offensive all day so he can't see it while Angela can. The logic is impeccable within Michael's deranged framework, which is what makes it so funny. It's also a callback to win-win-win, adding an additional layer. Strong character integration — this solution could only come from Michael.

jokes.text: Michael announces that Tuesdays/Thursdays is 'style three' — compromise — and 'it is not ideal.'
jokes.setup: Pam suggests a compromise (poster up on Tuesdays and Thursdays), which everyone finds reasonable.
jokes.punchline: Michael solemnly declares this to be the inferior 'style three' option and says it is 'not ideal' — his framework ranks compromise below a t-shirt solution.
jokes.explanation: A solid callback beat. The joke is that Michael's arbitrary ranking system makes him prefer his absurd t-shirt idea over the obviously sensible compromise. Functional.

jokes.text: Michael announces the answer is 'make the poster into a t-shirt' — his insane solution — and railroads everyone into accepting it.
jokes.setup: After laying out all options, Michael is supposed to let them choose.
jokes.punchline: He just declares the answer is his own worst idea and steamrolls the protest.
jokes.explanation: The joke is the gap between process and result — Michael runs an entire mediation framework and then just imposes his own worst idea anyway. The payoff is in the cringe of watching it happen.

jokes.text: Pam hand-delivers Angela's Save-the-Date — having not had her zip code — and Angela's talking head: 'It's not my taste.'
jokes.setup: Pam explains Angela didn't get her Save-the-Date because she didn't have her zip code.
jokes.punchline: Angela receives a hand-delivered Save-the-Date and her talking-head response is just 'It's not my taste' — a passive-aggressive dismissal of a kind gesture.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Angela character comedy. The hand delivery was a warm gesture; 'It's not my taste' is such a precisely Angela response — ungrateful, judgmental, and delivered without any apparent self-awareness. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Michael creates a conflict with Toby over the complaints file, then uses 'win-lose' to force Toby to hand it over.
jokes.setup: Toby refuses to show Michael the complaints file. Michael announces 'now you and I have a conflict' and orders Toby to give it to him.
jokes.punchline: Michael uses his own conflict framework to legitimize bullying Toby, then narrates 'I had to use win-lose on that. It was not pretty.' — treating an abuse of power as an unfortunate but necessary mediation outcome.
jokes.explanation: Strong structural joke. The mediation framework Michael invented is immediately weaponized to bully Toby, and Michael genuinely narrates it as a legitimate tool with regret ('not pretty'). The callback to his earlier framework adds depth. Character-specific: only Michael turns HR language into a personal power grab.

jokes.text: Toby has a standing Friday 4pm appointment with Dwight to file grievances against Jim. The box labeled as a 'special file in New York' is just a box in Toby's office.
jokes.setup: Michael discovers a box full of complaint forms.
jokes.punchline: Toby reveals he has a WEEKLY standing appointment with Dwight for Jim grievances, and the 'special file in New York' is just a cardboard box sitting right there.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent world-building comedy. The reveal that Dwight has been diligently filing weekly grievances for years — and Toby has been placating him with a fake 'New York file' — is a perfect encapsulation of both characters. It also sets up the entire second half of the episode. The mundanity of the cardboard box being the 'special file' is perfectly executed. High character integration for all three characters involved.

jokes.text: Creed's complaint: 'Creed is sick of looking at the redhead all day and wants a seat facing the receptionist.'
jokes.setup: Michael is reading through complaints from employees.
jokes.punchline: Creed's complaint is that he wants to face the receptionist — a casually creepy motivation delivered matter-of-factly by Michael, who adds 'Nice.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Creed economy. The complaint perfectly encapsulates his lecherous, oddly specific strangeness. The fact that Michael's editorial response is 'Nice' — validating the creepiness — makes it better. Only Creed. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'You will notice that not one of these complaints is against me.' Cut to: Toby revealing he has a separate folder for complaints against Michael — January through March alone.
jokes.setup: Michael boasts in a talking head that none of the complaints are directed at him.
jokes.punchline: Immediate cut to Toby explaining he has a SEPARATE folder just for Michael complaints — showing January through March as a thick stack.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured mockumentary cut. The juxtaposition between Michael's self-congratulatory claim and the immediate visual/verbal contradiction is the purest form of this show's comedic grammar. The 'January through March' detail — implying there are MORE folders — is the right amount of specificity. The structure here is near-flawless: maximum information, minimum words, maximum impact.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I love this place, and it pains me to see all of the negativity festering.' — Delivered as he's about to tear open a box of complaints and force everyone to confront them.
jokes.setup: Michael makes a heartfelt speech about caring for the office.
jokes.punchline: His solution to negativity festering is to expose all the complaints publicly — which is the opposite of resolution and will obviously make things worse.
jokes.explanation: Standard Michael irony — loving sentiment, catastrophic action. Functional but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: 'That's what she said.' — Michael reflexively using his catchphrase after Phyllis says 'You already did me.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis notes that Michael already handled her complaint.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis says 'You already did me' and Michael immediately fires back 'That's what she said.'
jokes.explanation: The TWSS gag scores higher when the setup is unintentional and organic, and here Phyllis's straight line is pretty good. Michael's reflexive use is perfectly timed. However, as a running gag, it's dependent on familiarity with the catchphrase — the joke itself is functional rather than crafted. The economy is perfect since it's a single line.

jokes.text: Toby: 'Redacted' just means whoever complained came to me later and withdrew it. There were a bunch of complaints about Dwight redacted about six months ago.
jokes.setup: Michael asks what 'redacted' means after finding a file of complaints with names removed.
jokes.punchline: Toby reveals a mass withdrawal of Dwight complaints exactly six months ago — coinciding (presumably) with the start of Angela and Dwight's relationship, implying Angela pressured people to withdraw complaints.
jokes.explanation: The joke is layered — the 'redacted' reveal builds on the previous beat about Angela never complaining about Dwight, now adding the implication that she may have engineered the withdrawal of others' complaints. It rewards attentive viewers. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Pam's complaint — 'Does she have to plan her wedding on office time? Shouldn't she do that at home?' — was already withdrawn, but Michael reads it aloud anyway.
jokes.setup: Michael finds a complaint about Pam but says it's withdrawn. Pam demands to know what it said.
jokes.punchline: He reads it aloud in front of everyone anyway — undermining the entire concept of a 'withdrawn' complaint — and Pam is publicly embarrassed.
jokes.explanation: The cringe is in Michael's complete failure to understand that 'withdrawn' means confidential. Functional but not a standout moment.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: 'I have this kind of big secret about Angela. And I've been really nice to her, and I haven't told anyone, and... What the hell!'
jokes.setup: The complaint about Pam is revealed. Pam is frustrated.
jokes.punchline: In talking head, she vents that she's been holding a big secret about Angela out of niceness — and now Angela complained about her. The implied threat to tell the secret (Angela/Dwight's relationship) is comedically restrained.
jokes.explanation: This is a great talking-head moment. The comedy is in Pam's barely-controlled indignation and the trailing '... What the hell!' as she contemplates whether to use what she knows. It's very human and very funny. Strong character integration — Pam's niceness being weaponized against her is a real tension.

jokes.text: Kelly: 'Ryan never returns my calls.' Michael: 'Join the club.' Ryan: 'My voicemail's real spotty sometimes.'
jokes.setup: Michael reads Kelly's complaint that Ryan never returns her calls.
jokes.punchline: Ryan's excuse is that his 'voicemail's real spotty sometimes' — a transparently thin excuse delivered with practiced casualness by someone clearly avoiding Kelly.
jokes.explanation: Ryan's excuse is pitch-perfect — it has the exact flavor of someone who has been caught but won't admit it. 'My voicemail's real spotty sometimes' is a very specific kind of bad lie. Michael's 'Join the club' is also a good beat. Strong economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Kelly: 'I didn't file a complaint. I was just talking.' Toby: 'To your HR representative.' Kelly: 'To my friend, I thought.'
jokes.setup: Kelly objects to her conversation with Toby being treated as a formal complaint.
jokes.punchline: Toby's correction — 'to your HR representative' — undercuts Kelly's naive belief that she was just chatting with a friend. The implication is also that Toby has no friends.
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one exchange: Kelly's obliviousness and the sad implication about Toby. The line 'To my friend, I thought' is genuinely touching and funny simultaneously. Very economical.

jokes.text: Dwight attempts to kiss Meredith (revealed complaint), then insists 'Redact it. Redact it.' while Meredith muses 'I'm not actually making a formal complaint. I just really think we should talk about it.'
jokes.setup: Meredith reveals during the group complaint session that Dwight tried to kiss her.
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately demands redaction, while Meredith's response is that she didn't file a formal complaint — she just 'really thinks they should talk about it' — a bizarrely calm approach to an HR incident.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the inversion — Meredith is oddly relaxed about what should be a serious incident, treating it like a personal conversation rather than an HR complaint. Dwight's panic ('Redact it!') vs. Meredith's calm curiosity is a good double act.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Question. When a name is withdrawn, does that also apply to the permanent misbehavior file in New York?' Toby: 'Sure.' — Dwight believing in the fictional 'permanent file in New York.'
jokes.setup: Dwight wants to know if redaction applies to the 'permanent misbehavior file in New York' — a file Toby invented to placate him.
jokes.punchline: Toby casually confirms it does — further maintaining the fiction — while the audience knows the 'special file in New York' is a cardboard box.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback. The joke works on two levels: Dwight's earnest belief in the fictional file, and Toby's complete willingness to maintain the lie. The 'Sure' from Toby is a perfect deadpan. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: 'Someone complained that the men's room is whites only.' Stanley: 'I didn't say that.' 'Then why is there a picture of a white man on the door.'
jokes.setup: Michael reads a complaint attributed to Stanley that the men's room is 'whites only.'
jokes.punchline: Stanley denies it, but Michael's follow-up — 'Then why is there a picture of a white man on the door' — reveals his complete inability to understand that a pictogram is not a racial designation.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Michael's inability to parse that a stick figure on a bathroom door is not a racial designation is perfectly calibrated. It's absurd but rooted in a kind of genuine stupidity that's specific to Michael. Stanley's flat denial makes it better. The economy is near-perfect — the whole joke lands in two lines. Highly quotable and lands as a genuine surprise.

jokes.text: Stanley says Phyllis cries too much and it bugs him. Phyllis: 'Stanley and I are close, too. We sit close.'
jokes.setup: Michael reads Stanley's complaint about Phyllis crying.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis's response — 'We sit close' — redefines 'close' in the most minimal possible terms, suggesting their 'closeness' is purely geographic.
jokes.explanation: A gem of economy. 'We sit close' is a three-word joke that perfectly captures Phyllis's sad social situation and her attempt to maintain dignity. The subversion of 'close' from emotional to physical proximity is sharp wordplay. Very quotable in context.

jokes.text: Jim asks about Roy's opinion on Pam's feelings. Pam: 'I try not to bother him about this kind of stuff.' Jim: 'You mean, like your thoughts and feelings.' Pam: 'Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are talking about the Angela situation. Jim asks what Roy thinks.
jokes.punchline: Pam says she doesn't 'bother' Roy with this — Jim rephrases it as 'your thoughts and feelings' — and Pam confirms, not catching the implied critique of her relationship.
jokes.explanation: This is quietly devastating and very well written. Jim's reframe — 'you mean, like your thoughts and feelings' — is a gentle indictment of Pam's relationship that she accepts without recognizing. On rewatch, knowing Jim's feelings for Pam, this lands even harder. The economy is excellent — the joke does enormous emotional work in very few words. Strong character integration for both.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's parking space non-resolution: 'I know you keep saying it's your space even though there's no assigned parking, but I keep forgetting.' 'Yes, that's the problem.' 'I guess so.' 'Okay. Well, all settled then.'
jokes.setup: Jim acknowledges he keeps parking in what Pam considers her space, even though there's no assigned parking.
jokes.punchline: His acknowledgment resolves nothing — he'll keep forgetting — and Pam knows it. Michael's 'all settled then' closes it as if anything happened.
jokes.explanation: Michael's 'all settled then' is the best part of this beat — he declares resolution where there is none. Functional but secondary.

jokes.text: Ryan: 'I don't like you.' — delivered directly to Michael.
jokes.setup: After the parking space non-resolution, Ryan addresses Michael directly.
jokes.punchline: Ryan simply says 'I don't like you' — four words of unusual directness in a setting where everyone else is being passive-aggressive. It's so blunt it becomes funny.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the contrast between the elaborate passive-aggression happening everywhere else and Ryan's total directness. Four words, maximum economy, perfectly Ryan.

jokes.text: Creed explains the 'distinct old man smell' by revealing he sprouts mung beans on damp paper towel in his desk drawer. 'Very nutritious, but they smell like death.'
jokes.setup: Ryan's complaint about Creed having a 'distinct old man smell' is read aloud.
jokes.punchline: Creed is not offended — he's helpful. He explains the smell is mung beans he's sprouting in his desk. 'Very nutritious, but they smell like death.'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke and one of Creed's signature moments. Everything about it works: the absurd specificity (mung beans, damp paper towel), the fact that Creed is not embarrassed but helpful, the casual admission that they 'smell like death' paired with 'very nutritious' — which treats these as acceptable tradeoffs. The joke operates perfectly without any setup beyond Ryan's complaint. Creed's complete lack of awareness that this is aberrant behavior is the engine. Maximum character integration. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Michael's solution to Kevin making sexually suggestive remarks to Angela: Angela must make sexually suggestive remarks to Kevin that will make HIM uncomfortable. 'I accept your decision.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is accused of making Angela uncomfortable with sexually suggestive remarks.
jokes.punchline: Michael's solution is symmetrical retaliation — Angela must now harass Kevin in kind. Kevin accepts this ruling enthusiastically.
jokes.explanation: The absurd logic of 'an eye for an eye' applied to workplace harassment is very funny — and Kevin's 'I accept your decision' suggests he's actively looking forward to this, which makes Angela's horror even more implied. Strong character comedy.

jokes.text: Jim suggests he and Dwight take their ID photo together to 'save time' — implying they could start carpooling.
jokes.setup: Jim casually suggests to Dwight that they take their ID photo together.
jokes.punchline: Jim's friendly suggestion — including meeting in the parking lot every morning to walk in together — is a perfectly targeted tease of Dwight who takes the bait.
jokes.explanation: A light Jim-teases-Dwight beat. The joke is Dwight saying 'Perfect' to something he'd normally find absurd. Functional.

jokes.text: Dwight refuses to smile for his ID photo. 'Showing one's teeth is a submission signal in primates. When someone smiles at me, all I see is a chimpanzee begging for its life.'
jokes.setup: The photographer asks Dwight to smile for his ID photo.
jokes.punchline: Dwight refuses and explains his deeply held belief that smiling is a primate submission signal, concluding that smiles look like 'a chimpanzee begging for its life.'
jokes.explanation: This is a top-tier Dwight joke and one of the most quotable moments in the episode. The pseudo-scientific anthropology angle is perfectly on-brand for Dwight, the escalation from 'submission signal in primates' to 'chimpanzee begging for its life' is well-constructed, and the delivery must be stone-cold serious. The joke is original, character-specific, and could be delivered by no one else. Excellent economy. Compares favorably to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Dwight's ID badge lists his middle name as 'Fart' instead of 'Kurt.' Michael narrates this to camera: 'What did I write?'
jokes.setup: Dwight looks at his ID badge and announces 'My middle name is Kurt, not Fart.'
jokes.punchline: Michael is shown looking at it and saying 'What did I write?' — implying he filled out the form himself and apparently wrote 'Fart' without noticing.
jokes.explanation: A good silly moment. 'What did I write?' is the right level of confusion. The visual of a security badge reading 'Fart' is inherently funny. Not sophisticated, but well-executed.

jokes.text: Dwight discovers Toby gave Jim the box of grievances. 'What box?' — Dwight's four years of complaints revealed to be sitting in an office box all along.
jokes.setup: Dwight tries to add to Jim's permanent file and is directed to Michael, who has the box.
jokes.punchline: Dwight asks 'What box?' — the dawning realization that his years of diligent complaint-filing went directly into a cardboard box in Toby's office.
jokes.explanation: A strong callback payoff. 'What box?' is the exact right response — the dawning horror of Dwight realizing the fiction. The dramatic irony (audience knows about the box) makes this land well.

jokes.text: Dwight's immediate nuclear ultimatum: 'I cannot work with Jim anymore. Either he goes or I go. You choose! Him or me!'
jokes.setup: Dwight discovers his complaint history has been ignored.
jokes.punchline: He immediately escalates to a full workplace ultimatum — either Jim goes or he goes — delivered with maximum drama over what are essentially pranks.
jokes.explanation: The disproportionality of Dwight's reaction is the joke. His theatrics are on-brand. Functional escalation comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight shows Jim a Stamford sales manager posting. 'Want me to call Jan and tell her you're interested? I could put in a good word for you 'cause I'll still be working here.'
jokes.setup: Michael gives Dwight until 5pm — implying Jim might be transferred — and Dwight immediately pivots to actively trying to get Jim out.
jokes.punchline: Dwight cheerfully offers to 'put in a good word' for Jim, transparently thrilled about the prospect of Jim leaving.
jokes.explanation: Rewatch bonus because this is foreshadowing Jim's actual transfer. Dwight's smug helpfulness is funny, and 'I'll still be working here' is a nice flourish. The dramatic irony adds value.

jokes.text: Dwight leading the office in chanting 'Transfer! Transfer! Transfer!' to get Jim moved to Stamford.
jokes.setup: Dwight is enthusiastically trying to get Jim transferred.
jokes.punchline: He starts a chant in the open office — 'Everybody! Transfer! Transfer! Transfer!' — as if rallying support for something the office cares about.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's absurd rally cry is funny. The image of him leading a chant is a good physical/visual beat. Solid.

jokes.text: The entire office chants 'Transfer! Transfer! Transfer!' when learning Jim might leave
jokes.setup: Dwight has found a Stamford posting for Jim
jokes.punchline: The full office immediately rallies behind the idea of Jim transferring — apparently everyone wants Jim gone, despite Jim being generally well-liked
jokes.explanation: The group chant is a good ensemble beat. The slight subversion of the expected emotional response (shouldn't people want Jim to stay?) makes it funnier. Again, enormous rewatch value given what actually happens.

jokes.text: Michael's cage match theory: 'Cage matches? Yeah, they work. How could they not work? If they didn't work, everybody would still be in the cage.'
jokes.setup: Michael is in the conference room trying to resolve the Jim/Dwight conflict.
jokes.punchline: Michael introduces cage matches as a conflict resolution method and defends the logic: if they didn't work, people would still be in them. This is circular reasoning presented as wisdom.
jokes.explanation: The logic of 'if they didn't work, everyone would still be in the cage' is beautifully stupid — it confuses 'getting out of the cage' with 'resolving the conflict.' It's the kind of reasoning that sounds almost coherent for a fraction of a second before collapsing entirely. Very quotable, strong character integration, well-constructed absurdist logic. Near-excellent.

jokes.text: Jim's grievances read aloud: crayons replacing pens, everyone calling Dwight 'Dwayne' for $5 each, a bloody glove planted in Dwight's desk with Jim claiming Dwight might be 'the real murderer.'
jokes.setup: Michael reads from Dwight's grievance file against Jim, which spans four years.
jokes.punchline: Each complaint reveals an elaborate, perfectly designed prank — the bloody glove/murder accusation is the apex.
jokes.explanation: The bloody glove/murder prank is the standout in this sequence — it takes Jim's pranks from annoying to genuinely deranged (in the best way). The escalation from 'crayons' to 'I think he may be the real murderer' is well-paced. The grievance file payoff delivers on its setup.

jokes.text: Jim's prank: telling Dwight there's an abandoned infant in the women's room. 'When I went to save the child, I saw Meredith on the can.' 'Gag.'
jokes.setup: Michael reads Dwight's complaint about the abandoned infant prank.
jokes.punchline: The prank doubled as a trap to get Dwight to walk in on Meredith in the bathroom. Dwight's written complaint includes 'Gag' — his parenthetical editorial.
jokes.explanation: The prank is funny in itself, but the word 'Gag' written into a formal HR complaint is the real joke — Dwight couldn't resist editorializing his own grievance. Strong character integration for both Jim (the elaborate setup) and Dwight (who took the bait and then documented it with a parenthetical 'Gag').

jokes.text: Jim's nickel prank: gradually adding nickels to Dwight's handset until he got used to the weight, then removing them all so Dwight knocked himself in the head with the phone.
jokes.setup: Michael reads the complaint: 'This morning I knocked myself in the head with the phone.'
jokes.punchline: Jim's talking-head explanation reveals the elaborate long-con — incrementally adding nickels over time until Dwight adapted, then removing them. 'That actually took a while.'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's greatest prank and one of the best Jim-pranks in the series. The genius is in the patience of the setup: Jim incrementally added weight over days or weeks until Dwight unconsciously adapted, then removed it all. The physical outcome (Dwight hitting himself in the head) is telegraphed but the METHOD is what's extraordinary. 'That actually took a while' is the perfect understated punchline — Jim saying it with quiet pride. Original, brilliantly structured, completely character-specific. Compares favorably to top-tier Office moments.

jokes.text: Jim's macro prank: every time Dwight typed his name, it printed 'diapers.'
jokes.setup: Michael reads: 'Every time I typed my name, it said diapers.'
jokes.punchline: Jim's talking head: 'Just a simple macro.' The casualness of 'just a simple macro' for something that would be deeply maddening to Dwight is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Just a simple macro' delivered with total nonchalance is perfect comedy economy. Jim's understated pride in his own work is a consistent comedic register that lands reliably.

jokes.text: Jim's desk prank: moving it one inch closer to the copier every time Dwight went to the bathroom. 'And that's how I spent my entire day, that day.'
jokes.setup: Michael reads: 'By the end of the day, my desk was about two feet closer to the copier.'
jokes.punchline: Jim explains he moved it an inch at a time all day. Then: 'And that's how I spent my entire day, that day.' — the confession that this consumed his entire workday.
jokes.explanation: The final sentence — 'And that's how I spent my entire day, that day' — is the joke within the joke. Jim just confessed that he devoted a full eight-hour workday to moving a desk two feet. The self-aware admission undercuts the prank's pranker status and makes him almost as absurd as Dwight. Very quotable, strong economy, excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head reflection: 'You know, these actually don't sound that funny, one after another. But he does deserve it, though.'
jokes.setup: Jim has been hearing his pranks read aloud as formal grievances.
jokes.punchline: Jim acknowledges that in the format of official complaints, the pranks have lost some of their humor — then immediately reaffirms they were warranted anyway.
jokes.explanation: This is a clever piece of meta-comedy. Jim essentially comments on the format of the scene itself — acknowledging that a grievance-list structure flattens comedy. Then the 'but he does deserve it, though' reestablishes his position with perfect Jim nonchalance. It works as self-aware comedy without breaking the fourth wall in a way that feels cheap. The rewatch bonus is high — it rewards viewers who are thinking about the structure of the scene.

jokes.text: Michael's shiatsu massage monologue: describes it as painful, people throw up, 'But the next day they feel great. I've never had one. They sound awful.'
jokes.setup: Michael is delivering a philosophical speech, presumably about conflict resolution, using shiatsu massage as a metaphor.
jokes.punchline: He builds up to 'but the next day they feel great' as the lesson — then immediately admits 'I've never had one. They sound awful.' — completely undermining the authority of his own metaphor.
jokes.explanation: Michael's self-undermining wisdom is a well-trodden comic avenue, but 'I've never had one. They sound awful.' is a particularly good execution of it. The structure — build-up, lesson, total reversal — works cleanly.

jokes.text: Jim and Dwight's shared talking head about whether Stamford would be good: 'It's a good market. Higher volume.' Dwight: 'Maybe we should both go.' Jim: 'I have a girlfriend.' Dwight: 'Sure you do, Dwight. Sure.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight are sitting together in a surprisingly collegial moment, talking about the Stamford opportunity.
jokes.punchline: Dwight suggests they both transfer; Jim deflects by saying he has a girlfriend. But then Jim calls Dwight 'Dwight' — appearing to confuse himself with Dwight — and says 'Sure you do.'
jokes.explanation: The unexpected warmth of this scene is itself part of the joke — the two enemies momentarily bonding — and then it deflates with Jim's misfire ('Sure you do, Dwight. Sure.') which seems to be directed at himself by accident. Rewatch bonus because this moment foreshadows the eventual transfer. Solid character comedy.

jokes.text: Michael bribes the photographer to stay for a group photo by offering $20, but then has to pay another $20 for a second attempt.
jokes.setup: Michael wants a group photo for the newsletter but the photographer can only be reimbursed for ID photos.
jokes.punchline: Michael pays $20 out of pocket for the photo, then the first attempt is apparently terrible, and the photographer demands another $20 for a second try — which Michael pays.
jokes.explanation: A decent situational beat but not especially inventive. The escalating cost is funny in a low-key way.

jokes.text: The group photo attempt — Michael announces 'we resolved a lot today, think happy thoughts' — reaction shot of the miserable group.
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to get the group to smile for a newsletter photo.
jokes.punchline: His 'think happy thoughts' speech lands on a group of people who are genuinely miserable — the visual of their non-smiling faces contradicts his optimism.
jokes.explanation: The visual is the joke — and the mockumentary format lets this land well. Functional irony.

jokes.text: Roy is revealed to have been the one who complained about Pam planning her wedding at the office — not Angela. 'I didn't know that Toby was going to write it down.'
jokes.setup: Pam has been furious at Angela for the complaint. Jim tells Pam not to take Angela's side.
jokes.punchline: Roy reveals he was the one who complained — a devastating misdirection that reframes both Pam's relationship issues and the complaint itself. His excuse is that he didn't think Toby would document it.
jokes.explanation: This is a structurally excellent joke that operates as both a comedic and emotional gut-punch. The misdirection (we expected Angela to be guilty) is well-sustained across the episode, and the reveal recontextualizes everything — including the Jim/Pam exchange about Roy not caring about Pam's feelings. 'I didn't know that Toby was going to write it down' is a perfect line: Roy's concern isn't that he hurt Pam, but that there's a paper trail. Strong callback, strong structure, high impact. Near top-tier for the episode.

jokes.text: Michael's Photoshop rescue of the terrible group photo: 'I'm sort of an expert at Photoshop, so it turned out fine in the end.'
jokes.setup: The group photo attempts have all been bad, and Michael has paid $160 total.
jokes.punchline: Michael reveals he's 'sort of an expert at Photoshop' and fixed it — implying a grotesque digital composite that he's proud of.
jokes.explanation: The implied visual of Michael's Photoshop 'expert' work is funny. His pride in the outcome is character-consistent. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael's voiceover: 'It was really hard getting a good picture of 15 people. He would not give me a discount, and eight tries added up.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just explained he's a Photoshop expert
jokes.punchline: The revelation that it took eight attempts — and Michael's grievance about not getting a bulk discount — is the callback punchline on the photographer bit
jokes.explanation: The $20 x 8 = $160 math is implied and funny; Michael's complaint about no discount is character-appropriate (he spent $160 on photos out of principle). Good button on a running bit.

jokes.text: Photographer trick: Michael says 'One, two...' and takes the photo without saying 'three', catching the group off guard
jokes.setup: Michael is counting down for yet another group photo attempt
jokes.punchline: He doesn't say 'three' — presumably producing a photo of people mid-anticipation
jokes.explanation: Standard photographer trick gag. Not especially crafted or character-specific; it's the kind of joke any sitcom could use. Functional.

jokes.text: Jim's voicemail to Pam about a 'doctor's appointment in the city' — revealed to be a meeting with Jan about the Stamford transfer.
jokes.setup: Jim leaves Pam a casual voicemail saying he has a doctor's appointment and won't be in until late afternoon.
jokes.punchline: Immediately cut to Jim at Jan's office, confirming he is interviewing for the Stamford position.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's emotional and structural climax presented as a comedic misdirection. Jim's cheerful, casual voicemail to Pam ('just thought I'd let you know') while he's actually at Jan's office is devastating in retrospect. The juxtaposition of the friendly voicemail with the reality of what he's doing is perfectly assembled. The rewatch value is enormous — this moment recontextualizes every Jim/Pam scene in the episode. Structure here is excellent mockumentary storytelling.

jokes.text: Michael's closing monologue: 'And that is why the idea of a cage match is so universally appealing. But here's the thing about cage matches, sometimes you have to open the cage. And that is something that Toby will never understand.'
jokes.setup: Michael is delivering his wrap-up wisdom about conflict resolution.
jokes.punchline: He returns to the cage match metaphor and delivers 'sometimes you have to open the cage' as a profound insight, then takes a parting shot at Toby — who has nothing to do with cage matches.
jokes.explanation: A solid closing joke. The callback to cage matches lands, and 'that is something that Toby will never understand' is a funny non-sequitur — Michael's contempt for Toby is so reflexive he brings him into an unrelated metaphor. The logic 'sometimes you have to open the cage' as a profound insight is appropriately absurd.

tmdb_overview: When Michael takes over conflict resolution duties from HR, chaos ensues at Dunder Mifflin.
